title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
description:
# Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix

Given an `m x n` integer matrix, return the length of the longest strictly increasing path in the matrix.

From a cell, you may move only to one of its four orthogonal neighbors: up, down, left, or right. You may not move diagonally, move outside the matrix, or wrap around the boundary. Every next cell on the path must have a value strictly greater than the current cell.

Path length counts visited cells; a one-cell path has length `1`.

## Example 1:

**Input:** matrix = [[9,9,4],[6,6,8],[2,1,1]]
**Output:** 4
**Explanation:** One longest increasing path has values `[1, 2, 6, 9]`.

## Example 2:

**Input:** matrix = [[3,4,5],[3,2,6],[2,2,1]]
**Output:** 4
**Explanation:** One longest increasing path has values `[3, 4, 5, 6]`. Moving diagonally is not allowed.

## Example 3:

**Input:** matrix = [[1]]
**Output:** 1

## Constraints:

* `m == matrix.length`
* `n == matrix[i].length`
* `1 <= m, n <= 200`
* `0 <= matrix[i][j] <= 2^31 - 1`

solutions.name: DFS Memoization on Cells
solutions.description:
## Approach

Treat each cell as the start of a path. A DFS from `(r, c)` tries only the four neighbors whose values are strictly larger, and memoizes the best path length starting from that cell.

## Key Insight

Strict increase makes the directed graph acyclic: a path can never return to a smaller or equal value. Therefore each cell's answer is computed once, even though many starts may reach it.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(m * n)
- Space Complexity: O(m * n)

solutions.name: Topological BFS from Local Minima
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build directed edges from a lower cell to a higher adjacent cell. Local minima have indegree zero, so Kahn's algorithm can peel the graph by increasing layers. The number of processed layers is the longest path length.

## Key Insight

Every edge moves from one layer to a later layer. Removing all current zero-indegree cells at once corresponds to taking one step along all possible increasing paths.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(m * n)
- Space Complexity: O(m * n)

solutions.name: Value-Sorted Dynamic Programming
solutions.description:
## Approach

Sort all cells by value in ascending order. When processing a cell, all smaller-valued neighbors have already received their best path lengths, so the current cell can extend the best smaller neighbor.

## Key Insight

The matrix is a DAG ordered by value, but equal values must not connect. Sorting makes that order explicit and avoids recursion and queue layer bookkeeping.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(m * n log(m * n))
- Space Complexity: O(m * n)

solutions.name: Reverse Topological BFS from Local Maxima
solutions.description:
## Approach

Count each cell's outgoing edges to larger neighbors. Cells with no larger neighbor are local maxima. Peel those maxima first, then move backward to smaller neighbors; the number of reverse layers is the longest increasing path length.

## Key Insight

This is the same DAG as the local-minimum topological sort, but viewed from sinks instead of sources. It is useful for teaching that the answer is a graph height independent of traversal direction.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(m * n)
- Space Complexity: O(m * n)

solutions.name: Explicit-Stack Postorder DFS
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the same memoized DFS recurrence, but replace recursive calls with an explicit stack. Each stack frame is visited once before its larger neighbors and once after those neighbors have memo values.

## Key Insight

A matrix can contain a very long increasing snake. The explicit stack teaches the same postorder dependency as recursion while avoiding Java call-stack depth risk on large inputs.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(m * n)
- Space Complexity: O(m * n)

tests.description: Canonical matrix has a longest increasing path of length four through 1,2,6,9.
Second example follows an increasing route ending at six.
Single cell boundary has path length one.
One-row increasing matrix has length two.
One-row decreasing left-to-right values can still be traversed from the low end.
One-column increasing matrix has length two.
Monotone grid still limits movement to adjacent cells, giving length five instead of nine.
Harder matrix requires turning through several cells to reach length six.
Flat matrix has no strictly increasing move, so the longest path is one.
Diagonal movement from 1 to 2 is not allowed.
A full snake path uses every cell exactly once.
Large integer values near the maximum must compare safely.
A valley feeding a snake path should not confuse local-greedy choices.
Zero-valued start and a two-row snake cover the lower bound and turns.
A larger winding route checks that multiple local choices are handled.
